939.title: The hardest gift
939.hook: the traditions speak of forgiveness, and none of them pretends it's easy
939.carry: sending a guard away from his post
939.howItsDone: Forgiveness is taught across the traditions: in Jewish practice around the Days of Awe, in Christian prayer, in Islamic teaching on pardon, and in Buddhist practices of loving-kindness, each with its own understanding of who forgives and how.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sabbath: finish, look, rest, the end of the weeks on work. Your line was work well, then rest.

Some names land like a small stone in the chest. A parent. An old friend. A business partner. An ex. Years go by, the stone is still there, and somebody says, kindly, just let it go. How, exactly? That question opens the next stretch of this path. For the coming weeks you'll hear what the traditions say about forgiveness: Jewish voices first, then others, one at a time. And before any of them speaks, one thing worth saying plainly: the texts ahead don't pretend it's easy.
screen: `A STONE IN THE CHEST.` → `JUST LET IT GO. HOW?` → `NOBODY SAYS IT'S EASY.`

segments.voice: First, why call it a gift. Forgiving gives something away: the right to get even, the story where you're owed. Nobody can force it out of you. That's what makes it a gift, and what makes it hard. Second, two old voices. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in one line: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love", and calls this an old rule. The Qur'an, in a verse about answering a wrong, allows a response in kind, then says that whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with God. Neither pretends the hurt didn't happen. Both point past it. Third, what forgiveness is not. Some teachers today, from more than one tradition, draw a line between forgiving and excusing. Forgiving doesn't say it was fine, or mean pretending to forget. For some, it doesn't mean walking back into the same room with the same person. The traditions draw these lines in different places: whether the one who did wrong has to ask first, who is able to forgive what, and whether forgiving means making up. Fourth, why it's hard. Anger is often doing a job. It guards a wound. It keeps a record, so the thing won't happen again. Asking it to stand down can feel like sending a guard away from his post. That's why, on this path, forgiveness is a practice, not a switch. It might take one try. It might take a great many.

segments.voice: Let one name come up, someone you haven't forgiven, not the biggest one, and notice what happens in the jaw, the chest, the hands. You don't have to forgive them now; just say the name quietly and let it sit beside you, like someone in the next seat of a bus. If you pray, you can bring that name into your prayer, just as it is.
Forgiveness. Giving up the claim to get even, freely given, never forced, and often slow. Today's word.

940.title: Teshuvah, the return
940.hook: Jewish repentance is a turning back, always possible
940.howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah all year, and especially in the month of Elul and the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur, when the liturgy returns again and again to turning back to God and repairing wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was forgiveness: giving up the claim to get even, freely, and often slowly. Your line was sending a guard away from his post.

A driver misses the exit. The map on the phone doesn't scold or replay the mistake. It just says: make a U-turn when possible. There's a quiet mercy in those last two words. When possible. The way back is still there, a little further down the road. Jewish tradition has a word for that kind of turn, and it's where these Jewish voices on forgiveness begin. Before anyone asks how to forgive someone else, this word asks something simpler: what happens when you're the one who went the wrong way?
screen: `A MISSED EXIT.` → `U-TURN WHEN POSSIBLE.` → `THE WAY BACK IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Teshuvah is usually translated repentance, but its plain meaning is return: a turning back, the way you'd turn toward home after walking the wrong way. The weight falls less on feeling terrible and more on turning around. Second, the prophets' call. Hosea, in the King James words: "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity." Fallen, yes. But the first word is return. Ezekiel goes further: the one who turns from wrongdoing and does what is right will live, and the old wrongs are not held against them. Then a line that sounds almost like a renovation: "make you a new heart and a new spirit." Third, a door older than the wrong. A tradition in the Talmud lists repentance among the things made before the world itself. Read one way, the way back was built before anyone had gone wrong. Fourth, small turns count. Teshuvah isn't only for great wrongs. Jewish teachers speak of it for habits too: the sharp tongue, the temper, the thing you do when you're tired. Turning once, in the moment, is already a return. It needn't wait for a holy day, though, as this week will show, a season of the year is set aside for it. The door, in this teaching, stays open.

Let that moment arrive in your mind, and this time make a quarter turn, one step back toward the person you meant to be. If you pray, you can bring this turning into your prayer, in your own words.

941.title: Four steps
941.hook: Maimonides: recognize it, regret it, confess it, resolve not to repeat it (Laws of Repentance 2)
941.carry: sorrow aimed at changing the future
941.howItsDone: Jews who follow Maimonides' teaching on teshuvah include a spoken confession, called viduy, in prayer, especially on Yom Kippur, alongside regret and a resolve to change.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was teshuvah: return, the U-turn that stays possible. Your line was return.

Some apologies have the shape of an apology and almost none of the inside. Sorry you feel that way. Mistakes were made. A quick sorry tossed over the shoulder on the way out. The difference is easy to hear, even when it's hard to say what's missing. Moses Maimonides, a rabbi, doctor and philosopher, wrote a code of Jewish law, and inside it a section called the Laws of Repentance. There he takes yesterday's return and lays it out step by step, so you can see what's missing.
screen: `SORRY YOU FEEL THAT WAY.` → `WHAT'S MISSING?` → `MAIMONIDES LAYS IT OUT.`

segments.voice: First, recognize it. You stop doing the thing, and you see it for what it was. Not a misunderstanding, not bad luck. A wrong, with your name on it. Second, regret it. Maimonides wants more than a shrug: the person regrets what they did, looking back and feeling sorry it happened. Sorrow about the past, aimed at changing the future. Third, confess it. The confession is spoken, said in words, out loud before God. A wrong said out loud, as a sentence, is harder to blur. Fourth, resolve. You decide not to do it again, and he says the commitment should be real enough that the One who knows the heart could vouch for it. Then he gives a test for when the return is complete. The same situation comes back: the same chance, the same strength, the same temptation. And this time the person doesn't do it, because they've changed, not because they couldn't. And one sharp image. Confessing without resolving to stop, Maimonides says, is like going into a purifying bath while still holding the very thing that made you impure. The water can't help while your hand is closed around it. These four steps, in his telling, are between a person and God. When the wrong was done to another person, there's something more, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `RECOGNIZE IT.` · `REGRET IT.` · `CONFESS IT ALOUD.` · `RESOLVE NOT TO REPEAT IT.` · then, large: `THE SAME CHANCE, AND YOU DON'T.`

segments.voice: Choose something small and real from this week, not the worst thing you've ever done, and walk it through the four steps: name it plainly, without excuses; feel its weight for a breath or two, no more; say it in a single whispered sentence, to God if you pray; and decide what you'll do when the same moment comes. Then breathe out, and let your hands open in your lap.

942.title: Ask them first
942.hook: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God; wrongs against people need their forgiveness (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
942.howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, some Jews seek out family, friends and colleagues to ask forgiveness directly, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day does not atone for wrongs against people until the person is reconciled.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was four steps: recognize, regret, confess, resolve. Your line was sorrow aimed at changing the future.

It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and a man has been in synagogue since the evening before. He's fasting, standing for the long prayers, beating his chest at every line of the confession. And somewhere across town is his sister, whom he hasn't spoken to since a bad argument last spring. He's been thinking about her all day. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, has a sentence for exactly this man. The day he's keeping can do a great deal. But there's one thing it won't do for him.
screen: `FASTING, PRAYING, CONFESSING.` → `A SISTER ACROSS TOWN.` → `ONE THING THE DAY WON'T DO.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the tractate on Yom Kippur, the Mishnah says it plainly: for wrongs between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, it does not atone, until the one who did wrong makes peace with the one they wronged. Second, where it comes from. The Mishnah names Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, reading a verse from Leviticus about the day. In the King James, the verse ends: "that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD." He reads those last words closely. Before the Lord. The day cleanses what lies between you and God. What lies between you and your sister stays where it is until you go to her. Third, how far you have to go. Maimonides, in his Laws of Repentance, makes it practical. You go to the person and ask. If they refuse, you go back with others, a second time and a third. If they still refuse, you may stop, and now the one refusing carries the fault. The asking is required. The answer is theirs. Fourth, why it matters. In the Mishnah's reading, God doesn't do your apologizing for you. The person you hurt isn't skipped over on the way to heaven. And so, on the day before Yom Kippur, some Jews make a point of calling, writing, or knocking on a door.

943.title: Joseph weeps
943.hook: Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him, and weeps (Genesis 45:1–15)
943.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Joseph and his brothers in the weekly Torah portions in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis too; it is often taught as a story of reconciliation within a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Yom Kippur: the day atones for some wrongs, but wrongs against people need the person. Your line was the answer is theirs.

Egypt, a room in the governor's house. The brothers from Canaan stand before the governor, terrified. A silver cup was found in the sack of the youngest, Benjamin, and now the governor means to keep him as a slave. Judah steps forward and offers himself instead. He can't go home without the boy, he says; it would kill their old father. What the brothers don't know is that the governor understands every word. He is Joseph, the brother they sold into slavery years ago. And he has just reached the end of what he can hold in.
screen: `A ROOM IN EGYPT.` → `JUDAH OFFERS HIMSELF.` → `THE GOVERNOR IS JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: First, the room empties. In the King James words: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me." Whatever happens next, he won't make his brothers face it in front of strangers. Second, the sound. "And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard." Earlier he turned away from them to weep, and once hurried out to a private room. This time he doesn't hide it. Then the plainest words: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He names exactly what they did. Third, what he does with it. The brothers can't answer. So Joseph tells them not to be grieved, nor angry with themselves, and says God sent him ahead to keep people alive through the famine. Readers disagree about this. Some hear deep forgiveness. Some notice he never says I forgive you, and that later in Genesis, after their father dies, the brothers are afraid all over again. The text lets both readings stand. Fourth, the last line. Joseph kisses each of them and weeps on them. Then: "and after that his brethren talked with him." After the tears, talking. It may be the whole point: years of silence, and then a family in one room, speaking again.
screen: `CAUSE EVERY MAN TO GO OUT.` · `HE WEPT ALOUD.` · `I AM JOSEPH YOUR BROTHER.` · `AFTER THAT, THEY TALKED.` · then, large: `HE WEPT ALOUD.`

If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are.

944.title: Esau runs
944.hook: twenty years after being cheated, Esau runs to embrace Jacob (Genesis 33:4)
944.howItsDone: Jews read the meeting of Jacob and Esau in the yearly cycle of Torah readings in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis; it is taught as a story of brothers reconciled after a deep wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Joseph weeps: a room emptied, a brother named, and then talking. Your line was he wept aloud.

Dust on the horizon. Jacob looks up, and there is his brother Esau with, the text says, four hundred men. The last time they were together, Jacob dressed up as Esau, fooled their blind father, and walked off with the blessing meant for his brother. Esau said in his heart that he would kill him. Jacob ran, and stayed away a long time; in his own words to his father-in-law, twenty years. Now he's coming home, limping from a night of wrestling by the river. He has sent gifts ahead, wave after wave, and split his camp in two in case one half is attacked. And now he walks out in front of them all.
screen: `DUST ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE STOLEN BLESSING.` → `JACOB WALKS OUT IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob bows. The King James says he "bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother." It's the posture of a man expecting the worst. Second, Esau runs. Here is the whole surprise, in one verse: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech first. No terms. No demand for an apology. The text never says what changed in Esau. It only shows us his feet. Third, the gifts. Jacob keeps pressing the flocks on him, and Esau waves them off: "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob insists: "Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee." Some readers notice the word. Blessing. The very thing he stole, and now he's trying to hand a blessing back. Fourth, a face. Jacob says: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God." The night before, he had wrestled until dawn and named the place for seeing God face to face. Now he says it of his brother. Readers have heard different things in that line. One reading: a face that should have been angry and is kind instead is about as close to the divine as it gets. The story doesn't tie a bow on it. The brothers soon part ways again. But for one morning, the wronged one ran.

945.title: The Days of Awe
945.hook: ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for making amends
945.howItsDone: During the Days of Awe, Jews pray special prayers, hear the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, give charity, and seek out people they have wronged to ask forgiveness before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Esau runs: the wronged brother moving first. Your line was he ran to meet him.

Two dates circled on a kitchen calendar. Next to the first, someone has drawn a little ram's horn. Next to the second, one word: fast. Between them, the squares are full of small notes. Call Mom. Coffee with Dan. Write to Mr. Levin. Return the drill. It looks like an ordinary to-do list. It isn't. It's a list of people. In the Jewish year, the stretch between those circles has a name, and it's built for exactly what this week has been about: turning back, and going to the people you've wronged.
screen: `TWO DATES CIRCLED.` → `A LIST OF PEOPLE.` → `A SEASON FOR TURNING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the calendar. Leviticus sets the two days. In the King James words: "In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation." That's the day Jews call Rosh Hashanah, the new year. Then: "Also on the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a day of atonement." Yom Kippur. From the first day to the tenth: ten days. In Hebrew they're the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe. Second, the picture. Tradition says, in a teaching in the Talmud, that on the new year the books are opened, and on the Day of Atonement they're sealed. Those in between have until then. It's an image, and readers hold it in different ways, but it gives the days their feel: a door that's open, and won't stay open forever. Third, the work. A prayer in the liturgy for these days names three things that turn aside the harsh decree: repentance, prayer and charity. Fourth, this whole week in one season. Forgiveness. The turn back. Maimonides' four steps. Asking the person first. Joseph weeping. Esau running. Joseph and Esau are read at other times of the year, but the turning, the steps and the asking all come due in these ten days: the apology that's been waiting, the call you keep putting off, made inside a window with a closing date.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY AND THE TENTH.` · `THE BOOKS OPEN, THEN CLOSE.` · `REPENTANCE, PRAYER, CHARITY.` · `THIS WEEK, IN ONE SEASON.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Open a blank page in your mind and let names arrive, one at a time, of people you owe something: an apology, an overdue thank-you, a call, a thing to return. Don't judge or rank the list; when no more come, look it over once, and give it a closing date ten days away. If you pray, you can hold the list in your prayer, in your own words.
Yamim Noraim. The ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, set aside for teshuvah, prayer, charity, and making amends. Today's word.
Your line: ten days. A door that's open, and won't stay open forever. See you tomorrow.
